title: What dangerous goods training is required to ship or handle cargo by air?
seoTitle: IATA and ICAO dangerous goods training
description: Competency-based dangerous goods training under the ICAO Technical Instructions and IATA DGR 1.5, recurrent within 24 months, and CASA and FAA rules.
shortAnswer: Anyone who prepares, accepts, handles or carries dangerous goods by air must be trained and assessed as competent for their function before performing it, under the International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) Technical Instructions and Subsection 1.5 of the International Air Transport Association (IATA) Dangerous Goods Regulations. Training covers general familiarization, function specific tasks and safety, follows a competency-based approach, and must be repeated within 24 months. Records are kept for at least 36 months.
keyTakeaways: ICAO Annex 18 requires dangerous goods to be carried in accordance with the Technical Instructions, which contain training requirements that apply to everyone involved in consigning, handling and carrying dangerous goods.

Under IATA DGR paragraph 1.5.1.2.1, employers must ensure personnel are competent for each function before performing it, through general familiarization, function specific and safety training with assessment.
Recurrent training is due within 24 months; CASA ties this to ICAO Technical Instructions Part 1;4.3 and DGR 1.5.1.3, and the FAA requires Part 121 hazmat training within the past 24 months.
Training and assessment records must include evidence of competence and be kept for at least 36 months from the most recent completion month (DGR 1.5.1.4, as summarized in IATA guidance).
The 68th edition of the DGR takes effect on January 1, 2027, incorporating the 2027 to 2028 ICAO Technical Instructions.
jurisdiction: International (ICAO and IATA), with Australian (Commonwealth) and United States (federal) implementation
regulator: International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) as standard setter; national authorities such as the Civil Aviation Safety Authority (CASA) and the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA). The International Air Transport Association (IATA) publishes the Dangerous Goods Regulations as an industry standard.
appliesTo: Shippers and packers who classify, pack, mark, label and document dangerous goods for air transport
Freight forwarders and ground handling agents that accept, store, build up or load dangerous goods
Aircraft operators, including cargo acceptance staff, load planners, flight crew and cabin crew
Passenger handling and screening staff who identify dangerous goods carried by passengers

sections.heading: Where do air dangerous goods training requirements come from?

blocks.text: The legal source is ICAO Annex 18 and the Technical Instructions for the Safe Transport of Dangerous Goods by Air (Doc 9284), applied in each country by its civil aviation authority. ICAO's [dangerous goods page](https://www.icao.int/safety/DangerousGoods/Pages/default.aspx) states that one of the Annex 18 Standards "requires that dangerous goods be carried in accordance with the Technical Instructions" and that the Technical Instructions "contain training requirements that apply to everyone involved in consigning, handling and carrying dangerous goods."

The IATA Dangerous Goods Regulations (DGR) sit alongside the Technical Instructions. IATA describes the DGR as a "field manual" version of the Technical Instructions and notes that airlines apply some requirements more strictly, so in practice most airlines will not accept a shipment that does not meet the DGR. The training rules are in DGR Subsection 1.5.

Because the DGR text itself is a paid publication, this page relies on IATA's freely published training guidance, national regulations that quote the requirements, and ICAO's public pages. Organizations should confirm details against the edition they hold.

sections.heading: What does competency-based dangerous goods training require?

blocks.text: It requires the employer to define the functions each person performs, train them to the competencies those functions need, and assess that they are competent before they do the work. IATA's [Dangerous Goods Training Guidance](https://www.iata.org/contentassets/90f8038b0eea42069554b2f4530f49ea/dgcbta-1-en.pdf) (Edition 1, January 1, 2023), which replaced the former DGR Appendix H, quotes DGR paragraph 1.5.1.2.1: the employer "must ensure that personnel are competent to perform any function for which they are responsible prior to performing any of these functions."
The guidance lists three mandatory training elements:

items: **General familiarization training:** familiarity with the general provisions.
**Function specific training:** training to competently perform the function the person is responsible for.
**Safety training:** recognizing the hazards presented by dangerous goods, safe handling, and emergency response procedures.

blocks.text: The guidance stresses that responsibilities "are determined by the specific functions the personnel perform and not by their job titles". A ground service agent who both accepts cargo and loads aircraft needs training for both functions. This is the same logic as [role-based training](/glossary/role-based-training), applied to a hazard where the consequence of a gap is an in-flight fire.

blocks.title: Outsourcing does not move the obligation
blocks.text: IATA's guidance states that if the training function is outsourced, employers remain responsible for determining the competencies their personnel need and for evaluating how well the training meets them.

sections.heading: How often must dangerous goods training be repeated?

blocks.text: Recurrent training must be completed within 24 months of the previous training. Australia's [CASA EX29/24](https://www.legislation.gov.au/F2024L00681/latest) instrument records that this "every 2 years" validity comes from ICAO Technical Instructions Part 1;4.3 and DGR section 1.5.1.3.

CASA EX29/24 exempts Australian aircraft operators, ground handling agents, freight forwarders, screening authorities and shippers from the strict two year rule in Part 92 of the Civil Aviation Safety Regulations 1998 (CASR), on conditions. Recurrent training must be done within 24 months from the end of the month of the last training, and training done in the final three months of that period does not shorten the next cycle. The instrument is repealed at the end of May 31, 2027, so operators using the extended window should plan for its expiry or replacement.

In the United States, [14 CFR 121.1005](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-121.1005) bars an air carrier from using any person in a hazardous materials job function unless they have completed its FAA approved initial or recurrent hazmat training "within the past 24 months". Under 121.1005(d), finishing recurrent hazmat training one month early or one month late is treated as finishing it in the month it fell due. A new hire may work for up to 30 days under direct visual supervision before initial training.

Shippers and forwarders in the United States are also covered by the general DOT hazmat employee training rule, which has its own three year cycle; see [DOT hazmat employee training](/regulations/dot-hazmat-employee-training). Where air transport is involved, building to the 24 month cycle meets both.

Records must show who was trained, when, on what material, by whom, and evidence that the person was assessed as competent. IATA's guidance summarizes DGR paragraph 1.5.1.4 as requiring the individual's name, the most recent training and assessment completion month, a description or reference to the materials used, the name and address of the training organization, and evidence of competence for each function.

Records must be retained "for a minimum period of 36 months from the most recent training and assessment completion month" and made available to the employee or national authority on request. US air carriers must keep records of training received in the preceding three years for as long as the person performs the function and for 90 days after, under [14 CFR 121.1007](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-14/section-121.1007), including a copy of the certification showing a test was completed satisfactorily.

sections.heading: How can employers map dangerous goods training to roles and evidence?

blocks.text: Air cargo staff are trained by function, so the useful unit of planning is the function, not the department. Built from the sources on this page, the table pairs typical functions with the training elements, the cycle and the records a civil aviation authority inspector or airline auditor is likely to ask for.

blocks.text: Mapping functions rather than job titles is what makes this auditable. The approach is the same as the one in [how to build a training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix), with assessment evidence designed using [how to design competency assessments](/guides/how-to-design-competency-assessments).

The IATA DGR is reissued every January. According to IATA's [DGR program page](https://www.iata.org/en/programs/cargo/dgr/), the 68th edition takes effect on January 1, 2027, and its [significant changes summary](https://www.iata.org/contentassets/9dece0d6bb3c41d2bd95456b18215908/dgr-68-en-significant-changes.pdf) says it incorporates the ICAO amendments developed for the 2027 to 2028 edition of the Technical Instructions.

Changes with training impact include clarification that operators' manuals must be kept up to date (1.4.2), new operator duties around dangerous goods that require operator approval (1.4.3), and tighter passenger rules: power banks over 100 Wh are forbidden for passengers and crew, and passengers are limited to two power banks. IATA also notes an ICAO addendum on power banks issued on March 27, 2026. As at November 2026, passenger handling and cabin crew content should be reviewed before January 1, 2027.

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry starts from the function list in DGR Subsection 1.5 and the employer's own job task analysis, then defines the competencies and assessment points for each function before course material is written. When a new DGR edition is issued, the changed provisions can be traced to the functions and assessments they affect.

faqs.q: Is IATA dangerous goods training legally required?
faqs.a: The legal requirement comes from the ICAO Technical Instructions as applied by national regulators, such as CASR Part 92 in Australia and 14 CFR Part 121 Subpart Z for US air carriers. The IATA DGR is an industry standard, but airlines generally require shipments to comply with it, so training to the DGR is commercially necessary.

faqs.q: Can someone handle dangerous goods before completing training?
faqs.a: The DGR requires competence before performing a function. US rules allow a new hire or person changing function to work for up to 30 days under the direct visual supervision of a trained person, with a written record. Other authorities may not allow this, so check national rules.

faqs.q: Does a course certificate prove competence?
faqs.a: Not on its own under the competency-based approach. IATA's guidance says the training record must include evidence that personnel have been assessed as competent for each function they are responsible for. A generic course certificate without function specific assessment may not satisfy an auditor.

faqs.q: Is the 24 month recurrent period counted from the exact date?
faqs.a: Under the standard rule it runs from the previous training. CASA EX29/24 allows Australian entities to count to the end of the month, with protection for training done in the final three months, until May 31, 2027. US Part 121 carriers may complete training in the month before or after the due month.
